narrative: The model estimates a 66% chance that you will leave your job, meaning leaving is judged more likely than staying; on that basis, the promotion decision was negative. Gender, age, and health issues were not used in this prediction. The strongest signal was that you have other job opportunities: unlike most comparable employees predicted to stay, you reported receiving them, and this was the top factor pushing the prediction toward leaving. Your total career experience was the second strongest factor. With 11 or more years of experience—well above the typical staying employee, only about 15% of whom fall in that group—the model treated your profile as more mobile and likely to move. Your sector also ranked third: working in a sector classified as “other” was more common among leavers than among the staying comparison group (about 22% of stayers), so it added further weight toward leaving. Other aspects of your profile, such as your master’s degree, long tenure in this organization, overtime, low job support, and psychological exhaustion, were not among the top three drivers, so they did not outweigh these signals. Before reconsidering promotion, discuss concrete retention steps: clarify career paths and internal opportunities, review workload and support, and explore whether your external options reflect unmet development or recognition needs. A promotion decision should not rest on a prediction alone; use it as a prompt for a direct conversation about your intentions and the conditions that would keep you engaged.
